title: Divisibility by the Carmichael Function: Classification Across Integer Shift
content: The divisibility of integer shifts by multiplicative functions has long been a central topic in analytic number theory, originating from Lehmer’s study of φ(n) | n − 1 and later refinements concerning φ(n) | n + a. While extensive progress has been made for the Euler totient function, analogous questions for the Carmichael function λ(n) have remained largely inaccessible to existing techniques, particularly for fixed positive shifts a > 1. This paper investigates the divisibility relation λ(n) | n + a, establishing that for every fixed integer a ≥ 2 the set of such integers n has natural density zero unconditionally, and is finite under standard equidistribution assumptions on primes in square-modulus progressions, such as the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture. The argument combines structural and analytic methods. A valuation obstruction shows that for squarefree integers with sufficiently many prime factors, divisibility fails whenever a prime power divides λ(n) to higher order than it divides n + a. Analytic input from the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem controls the distribution of small prime divisors of pi − 1, while stronger equidistribution hypotheses are used to force the appearance of squared prime factors and trigger the obstruction. The only remaining configuration is an exceptional schema in which all prime divisors pi of n satisfy pi ≡ 1 (mod M ) with M | (a + 1) and pi − 1 squarefree, a case shown to yield at most one admissible prime for each modulus. Together these results provide a complete structural classification of the divisibility condition λ(n) | n + a across integer shifts, highlighting the finiteness of all positive shifts a ≥ 2, the contrasting behavior of the case a = 1, and the existence of infinite families for negative shifts. The methods extend naturally to other multiplicative functions, suggesting a broader framework for shifted divisibility phenomena. Extensive computational verification for all n ≤ 2 × 106 finds no counterexamples, providing strong numerical support for the theoretical conclusions.
